items.en: The Ten Perceptions: The Impurity of Food, and a World With No Delight
items.zh: 十想 · 食不淨想 · 一切世間不可樂想

zh: 四、食不淨想者，行者雖知無常、苦、空、無我，若於飲食猶生貪著，當修食不淨想以為對治。諦觀此食皆是不淨因緣故有，如肉是精血水道中生，是為膿蟲住處；如酥乳酪，血變所成，與爛膿無異；飯似白蟲，羹如糞汁。一切飯食，厨人執作，污垢不淨，若著口中，腦有爛涎，二道流下，與唾和合，然後成味，其狀如吐，從腹門入，地持，水爛，風動，火煮。如釜熟糜，滓濁下沈，清者在上。譬如釀酒，滓濁者為屎，清者為尿。腰有三孔，風吹膿汁，散入百脈，先與血和合，凝變為肉；從新肉生脂、骨、髓，以是因緣，故生身根。
en: Fourth, the perception of the impurity of food: the practitioner, though already knowing impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self, may still give rise to craving and attachment toward food and drink — one should therefore cultivate the perception of the impurity of food as its own antidote. Closely contemplate that this food exists, in every case, through causes and conditions that are themselves impure: meat, for instance, arises within the channels of semen and blood, itself a dwelling-place for pus and worms; ghee and dairy curds, transformed from blood, differ not at all from festering pus; cooked rice resembles white maggots, and broth resembles the liquid of excrement. Every meal, prepared and handled by the kitchen worker, is filthy and impure; once placed within the mouth, the brain's own decaying fluid flows down through its two channels, mingling with saliva, and only then does it form a taste — its very appearance resembling vomit. Descending through the body's gate into the belly, it is held by earth, decomposed by water, stirred by wind, and cooked by fire — like porridge simmering in a pot, its dregs and sediment sinking down while the clear part rises above; or like the brewing of wine, whose dregs and sediment become excrement, and whose clear part becomes urine.

The waist has three openings, through which wind blows the pus-like fluid, scattering it into the hundred vessels, where it first mingles with blood and congeals, transforming into flesh; from this fresh flesh, fat, bone, and marrow are then generated — and, through these very causes and conditions, the physical faculty of the body itself is produced.

zh: 從新舊肉令生五情根，從此五根則生五識，次第生意識，分別取相，籌量好醜，然後生我、我所心等諸煩惱及諸罪業。觀食如是本末因緣，種種不淨，知內四大與外四大則無有異，但以我見力故，強計為我有。行者如是思惟，知食罪過，若我貪著，當墮地獄、餓鬼，吞熱鐵丸，或墮畜生猪狗之中，噉食糞穢。如是觀食，則生厭想；因厭食故，五欲亦薄，即是食不淨想。
en: From this fresh and older flesh together, the five faculties of feeling are then generated; from these five faculties, the five sense-consciousnesses then arise, followed in turn by mind-consciousness, which distinguishes and grasps at marks, weighing and judging good and ill — and only afterward does the mind of self and what-belongs-to-self arise, together with every affliction and every unwholesome deed that follows from it. Contemplating food in this way, from its very origin through to its end, its causes and conditions manifold and impure throughout, one knows that the four elements within the body and the four elements outside it are, in truth, no different from one another — it is only through the sheer force of the view of self that one insists on reckoning it as belonging to oneself.

The practitioner, reflecting in this way, comes to know the fault inherent in food — should I still crave and cling to it, I am bound to fall into hell or among the hungry ghosts, swallowing balls of molten iron, or to fall among the animals, among pigs and dogs, devouring filth and excrement. Contemplating food in this way, weariness thereupon arises; and, through this very weariness toward food, the five desires, too, grow thin — this is precisely the perception of the impurity of food.

zh: 五、一切世間不可樂想者，行者若念世間色欲、滋味、眷屬、親里、服飾、園觀、國土、人事等，則生樂想，惡覺不息，障離欲道故。行者應當深心諦觀世間過罪之相。過罪有二種：一者、眾生；二者、國土。眾生過罪者，一切眾生皆有八苦之患，無可貪著。復觀眾生貪欲多故，不擇好醜，猶如禽獸；瞋恚重故，乃至不受佛語，不敬聞法，不畏惡道；愚癡多故，所求不以道理，不識尊卑；或慳貪、憍慢、嫉妬、很戾、諂誑、讒賊、邪見、無信、不識恩義；或罪業多故，造作五逆，不敬三寶，輕蔑善人。世間眾生善者甚少，弊惡者多，深觀如是煩惱過罪，應生厭離，如是不可親厚。
en: Fifth, the perception that nothing in the whole world is to be delighted in: should the practitioner call to mind the world's own sensual desire, its flavors, one's own family and kin, adornment and dress, gardens and parks, one's own homeland, and worldly affairs, a perception of pleasure thereupon arises, unwholesome thought never ceasing, obstructing the very path of freedom from desire. The practitioner should therefore, with a deep and earnest mind, closely contemplate the mark of the world's own manifold faults.

These faults are of two kinds: first, those belonging to sentient beings; second, those belonging to the land itself. As for the faults belonging to sentient beings: every sentient being is beset by the affliction of the eight sufferings, nothing in them worth craving or clinging to. One further contemplates that, since sentient beings are so given to craving and desire, they choose neither good nor ill, no different from beasts; since they are so given to heavy anger and hatred, they refuse even to accept the Buddha's own words, show no reverence in hearing the Dharma, and hold no fear of the evil destinies; since they are so given to heavy folly, what they seek follows no principle at all, unable even to distinguish the honored from the lowly; some are stingy and greedy, arrogant and conceited, envious and jealous, perverse and contrary, flattering and deceitful, slanderous and treacherous, holding wrong views, without faith, unable to recognize a debt of kindness; some, so given to heavy unwholesome deeds, commit the five heinous acts, show no reverence for the Three Jewels, and hold the virtuous in contempt. Among the sentient beings of this world, those who are good are exceedingly few, while the corrupt and evil are many — deeply contemplating afflictions and faults of this kind, one ought to give rise to weariness and detachment, recognizing that such beings are not to be drawn close to or cherished.

zh:
或有國多寒，或有國多熱，
有國無救護，或有國多惡，
有國多饑餓，或有國多病，
有國不修福，如是無樂處。
行者深觀欲界惡事如是，無有樂處，乃至上二界果報破壞時，憂苦甚於下界，譬如極高處墮落，摧碎爛壞。經言：「三界無安，猶如火宅，眾苦充滿，甚可怖畏。」若常觀是相，則深生厭離，愛覺不生，是名世間不可樂想。
en: As for the faults belonging to the land itself, the verse says:

"In some lands there is great cold, in some lands there is great heat;
some lands offer no refuge or protection, some lands are rife with evil;
some lands suffer great famine, some lands are rife with sickness;
some lands cultivate no merit at all — lands such as these hold no place of joy."

The practitioner, deeply contemplating the desire realm's own evils in this way, finds no place of joy whatsoever within it — and, further still, when the retribution belonging to the two higher realms themselves comes to ruin, its sorrow and suffering exceed even that of the lower realm, like a fall from the very greatest height, shattering and crushing all the more upon landing. The sutra says: "The three realms hold no peace at all, like a house already ablaze, filled everywhere with manifold sufferings, utterly to be feared." Should one constantly contemplate this mark, deep weariness and detachment thereby arise, and the thought of craving no longer arises at all — this is named the perception that nothing in the whole world is to be delighted in.

The digestion narrative — food traced from raw ingredient through mouth, stomach, and the body's own internal alchemy of the four elements into flesh, fat, bone, and marrow — mirrors the embryology and organ-anatomy passages from fascicle 8's root world, but redirects the same clinical, unflinching attentiveness toward an object most practitioners would never think to examine this closely: dinner. The fifth perception's own two-part structure (faults of beings, then faults of the land) reframes the nine contemplations' single corpse into something civilizational in scope — not one body's decay, but the moral failings of beings (the good, the text says, are exceedingly few and the corrupt many), and every land's shared hardship — culminating in the sūtra passage it quotes, the three realms as a "burning house," the same image found in the Lotus Sūtra's famous parable.

items.en: The Ten Perceptions: Death, Impurity, Cessation, Detachment, Exhaustion
items.zh: 十想 · 死想不淨想斷想離想盡想

zh: 六、死想者，行者若修上來諸想，多少懈怠心生，不能疾斷漏，是時應須深修死想。如佛說死想義：有一比丘偏袒白佛：「我能修死想。」佛言：「汝云何修？」比丘言：「我不望一歲活。」佛言：「汝為放逸修死想者。」復有比丘言：「我不望七月活。」有比丘言七日、六日、五日、四日、三日、二日活。佛言：「汝等皆是放逸修死想者。」有比丘言：「從旦至食。」有一比丘言：「一食頃。」佛言：「汝等皆是放逸修死想者。」有一比丘偏袒白佛言：「我於出息不保入息，入息不保出息。」佛言：「善哉！善哉！是真修死想者，是真不放逸行。」若能如是修死想者，當知是人破懈怠賊，一切善法恒得現前，是名修死想也。
en: Sixth, the perception of death: should the practitioner, having cultivated all of the perceptions given above, find some measure of laxity arising in the mind, unable to swiftly sever the contaminants, at such a time one should deeply cultivate the perception of death. As the Buddha explains the sense of the perception of death: there was a monk who, baring one shoulder, addressed the Buddha: "I am able to cultivate the perception of death." The Buddha said: "How do you cultivate it?" The monk said: "I do not expect to live out the year." The Buddha said: "You are one who cultivates the perception of death negligently." There was another monk who said: "I do not expect to live out seven months." Other monks said seven days, six days, five days, four days, three days, two days. The Buddha said: "All of you are cultivating the perception of death negligently." A monk said: "From dawn until the morning meal." Another monk said: "The space of a single meal." The Buddha said: "All of you, too, are cultivating the perception of death negligently." Then there was a monk who, baring one shoulder, addressed the Buddha, saying: "For my part, upon breathing out, I do not presume upon breathing in again; upon breathing in, I do not presume upon breathing out again." The Buddha said: "Excellent! Excellent! This is the true cultivation of the perception of death — this is true, unfailing diligence." Should one be able to cultivate the perception of death in just this way, one should know that this person breaks the bandit of laxity, and every wholesome dharma comes constantly to manifest before them — this is named cultivating the perception of death.

zh: 七、不淨想者，如前通明觀，見身三十六物五種不淨，是中應廣說。八斷想、九離想、十盡想者，緣涅槃，斷煩惱結使，故名斷想；離結使故，故名為離想；盡諸結使，故名為盡想。
en: Seventh, the perception of impurity: as already given above, within the thorough-and-bright contemplation, seeing the body's thirty-six substances and five kinds of impurity — the matter should be explained at length there.

Eighth, the perception of cessation; ninth, the perception of detachment; tenth, the perception of exhaustion: taking nirvāṇa as the object, severing the fetters of affliction, this is named the perception of cessation; being free of the fetters, this is named the perception of detachment; exhausting every one of the fetters entirely, this is named the perception of exhaustion.

zh: 問曰：若爾者，一想便足，何故說三？答曰：如前一法三說，無常即苦，苦即無我，此想亦如是。斷想，有餘涅槃；盡想，無餘涅槃；離想，二涅槃方便門。當知壞法人成就十想即成阿羅漢，具足二種涅槃，故說九想、十想為壞法道也。十想義種種分別，具如《摩訶衍》中廣說。
en: Question: if this is so, a single perception alone ought to suffice — why, then, are three spoken of? Answer: just as the single dharma spoken of before as three — impermanence is itself suffering, suffering is itself no-self — this perception, too, is just the same. The perception of cessation corresponds to nirvāṇa with remainder; the perception of exhaustion corresponds to nirvāṇa without remainder; the perception of detachment is the skillful gateway common to both kinds of nirvāṇa. One should know, then, that the practitioner of the destructive path, accomplishing the ten perceptions, thereby becomes an arhat, complete with both kinds of nirvāṇa — hence the nine contemplations and the ten perceptions together are spoken of as the destructive path. The sense of the ten perceptions, distinguished in every such way, is explained at greater length in the Mahāyāna treatise.

The Buddha's own dialogue with the monks is a small masterpiece of escalating standards — each answer sounds, on its face, like genuine urgency (who plans on living only a week?), and each is dismissed as "negligent" all the same, until the final monk names the only interval that isn't, in principle, presumptuous: the gap between one breath and the next. It's the same breath-based method (ānāpāna) that has anchored nearly every practice in this treatise since fascicle 3, now repurposed as the measuring stick for how seriously one takes death itself. The three-way split of cessation, exhaustion, and detachment, mapping respectively onto nirvāṇa-with-remainder, nirvāṇa-without-remainder, and the skillful gateway to both, closes the ten perceptions on the same doctrinal point that closed the nine contemplations: a threefold analysis of what is, at bottom, a single realization.

items.en: The Ten Perceptions and the Path — Closing Fascicle Nine
items.zh: 十想 · 趣道 · 卷第九竟

zh: 第三、明趣道相者，即有三種：一者、漸次入壞法道，具如前說。二者、非次第壞法道。從初發心即具修十想，斷諸結使，得阿羅漢果，具足二種涅槃，故《摩訶衍》云：「若於煖、頂、忍、世間第一法，正智慧觀，離諸煩惱，是離想；得無漏道，斷結使，是斷想；入涅槃時，滅五受陰，不復相續，是名盡想。」當知從初乾慧地來，即說離想等，此則異前所說。三想併在後無學道中也。
en: Third, clarifying the mark of how the ten perceptions lead toward the path: this, too, is of three kinds.
First, gradually entering the destructive path in sequence — this is entirely as already explained above.

Second, the destructive path entered out of sequence: from the very first arousal of the mind, one already cultivates the ten perceptions complete, severing every fetter, obtaining the fruit of arhatship, and becoming complete with both kinds of nirvāṇa. Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Within the stages of heat, summit, forbearance, and the supreme mundane dharma, correct wisdom's own contemplation, freeing one from every affliction — this is the perception of detachment; obtaining the undefiled path and severing the fetters — this is the perception of cessation; and, upon entering nirvāṇa, extinguishing the five aggregates of clinging so that they never again continue — this is named the perception of exhaustion." One should know, then, that, from the very stage of dry wisdom onward, the perception of detachment and the rest are already spoken of here — this differs from what was explained before, where the three perceptions were placed together within the later path of no-more-learning alone.

zh: 三者、隨分入道。若於十想之中隨修一想，善得成就，即能斷三界結使，得阿羅漢，證二種涅槃。故經云：「善修無常，能斷一切欲愛、色愛、無色愛，掉、慢、無明三界結使永盡無餘。」當知無常即是具足入道不煩惱想，下九想亦當如是一一分別趣道之相。復次，菩薩摩訶薩行菩薩道時，心廣大故，欲為一切眾生習甘露法藥，雖知諸法畢竟空寂，而亦具足成就十想。是菩薩於一一想中，次第入一切法門，旋轉無閡，為眾生說，當知十想即是菩薩摩訶衍也。
釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第九
en: Third, entering the path according to one's own portion: should one, among the ten perceptions, cultivate even a single one, skillfully bringing it to accomplishment, one is thereby able to sever the fetters of the three realms, obtain arhatship, and realize both kinds of nirvāṇa. Hence the sutra says: "Skillfully cultivating impermanence, one is able to sever every craving for the desire, form, and formless realms, and the fetters of agitation, conceit, and ignorance belonging to the three realms are extinguished forever, without remainder." One should know, then, that the perception of impermanence is itself already complete and sufficient for entering the path, free of affliction; the remaining nine perceptions, too, should each in turn be distinguished in this same way, with respect to the mark of how they lead toward the path.

Furthermore, when the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path, the mind being vast and expansive, wishing to prepare the ambrosial dharma-medicine for every sentient being, although knowing that every dharma is, in the end, empty and still, nonetheless becomes complete with the accomplishment of all ten perceptions as well. This bodhisattva, within each and every perception, enters every dharma-gate in turn, circling through them without any obstruction whatsoever, expounding them for the sake of sentient beings. One should know, then, that the ten perceptions are themselves precisely the bodhisattva's own Mahāyāna.
Shi Chan Boluomi Cidi Famen, Fascicle Nine, ends here.

The three approaches to the path — strictly sequential, front-loaded (all ten perceptions cultivated from the very start), and partial (any single perception, skillfully accomplished, sufficing on its own) — mirror the "difference and no difference" framing that opened the whole fascicle's treatment of the nine contemplations versus the ten perceptions: the treatise consistently refuses to present a single practice ladder as the only valid one, instead mapping out several legitimate routes to the identical destination. The fascicle's closing gesture is now a familiar one, echoing the nine contemplations, the eight recollections, the six wondrous gates, and the thorough-and-bright contemplation before it: every dharma-gate in this treatise, however narrow or visceral its starting point, turns out to be "the bodhisattva's own Mahāyāna" once fully realized.

quiz.q: In the impurity of food, how are meat, dairy, rice, and broth seen?
options: meat from semen and blood, a home for worms; dairy from blood like pus; rice like white maggots; broth like liquid excrement
quiz.why: Meat arises in the channels of semen and blood and houses worms; dairy is transformed blood like festering pus; rice resembles white maggots, broth liquid excrement.

quiz.q: Once food enters the belly, with what is its separation compared?
options: like porridge settling in a pot; like brewing wine, dregs becoming excrement and clear liquid urine
quiz.why: Held by earth, decomposed by water, stirred by wind, cooked by fire, it is like porridge in a pot, dregs sinking and clear rising; like wine-brewing, dregs become excrement and the clear part urine.

quiz.q: After contemplating food, what does one know about the inner and outer elements, and why does one still claim them?
options: they do not differ; only the force of self-view claims them as mine
quiz.why: Contemplating food from origin to end, one knows the elements inside and outside the body do not differ; only the force of self-view claims them as mine.

quiz.q: Of what two kinds are the world's faults?
options: those of beings and of lands
quiz.why: The faults are of beings (the eight sufferings, greed, anger, delusion) and of lands (cold, heat, famine, sickness).

quiz.q: When the two higher realms' rewards come to ruin, how great is the sorrow, and what simile is used?
options: worse than the lower realm, like falling from the greatest height and shattering
quiz.why: When the higher realms' rewards end, the suffering exceeds the lower realm's, like falling from the highest place and being crushed.

quiz.q: How does the cited sūtra describe the three realms?
options: no peace, like a burning house, full of suffering, to be feared
quiz.why: The three realms hold no peace, like a burning house full of suffering; constantly contemplating this brings weariness, which is the perception that nothing in the world is to be delighted in.

quiz.q: Which monk did the Buddha praise as truly cultivating the perception of death?
options: the one who did not count on the next breath
quiz.why: All who spoke of a year, months, days, or a meal were called negligent; only the monk who did not count on the next breath was praised as truly cultivating it.

quiz.q: To what do the perceptions of cessation, detachment, and exhaustion correspond?
options: cessation: with remainder; exhaustion: without remainder; detachment: the gateway to both
quiz.why: Cessation corresponds to nirvāṇa with remainder, exhaustion to nirvāṇa without remainder, and detachment to the expedient gateway to both.

quiz.q: What are the three ways the ten perceptions lead to the path?
options: gradual, out of sequence, and according to one's portion
quiz.why: The ten lead gradually along the destructive path, out of sequence from the first arousal, or according to one's portion, where even one perception suffices.

quiz.q: How does the out-of-sequence destructive path differ from the earlier sequence?
options: detachment and the rest are spoken of from the dry-wisdom stage, unlike placing all three in the final stage
quiz.why: Here detachment and the rest are spoken of from the stage of dry wisdom onward, unlike before, where all three were placed together in the path of no-more-learning.
